_meta.description: SAP attack-path templates. CONTENT, not code: a new path is a new entry here, never a code change. Each template names the checks that evidence each hop, so every hop is grounded in a check that already exists and a path can never claim more than the scanner actually detected.
_meta.how_a_path_instantiates: Every REQUIRED hop must have at least one OPEN finding in the landscape. Optional hops enrich a path but do not gate it. A path is therefore a statement that these conditions CO-EXIST, derived from exported configuration — never a claim that anything was traversed or validated. The console must say so.
_meta.cut_semantics: A hop marked cut=true appears on every variant of the path, so closing it disconnects the path. Non-cut hops reduce exploitability without severing it. This is the mitigate-vs-additional split: it needs no clever algorithm, only that each hop knows whether removing it disconnects.
_meta.targets_are_fair_scenarios: Each path ends at a scenario id from data/fair_scenarios.json, so a path terminates in a currency figure rather than a severity word.

paths.name: Lower-tier trust pivot into production
paths.summary: A non-production system holds a stored-credential or trusted RFC route into production, and the landing authorization is broad enough to act on arrival.
paths.narrative: Development and QA systems are routinely less controlled than production, yet a trusted-RFC relationship or a destination carrying stored credentials gives them a route in. Where the target's S_RFCACL is wildcarded, the caller can arrive as any user. This is the demo path: today these appear as unrelated rows across four modules and four severity bands.

hops.name: Route from a lower tier exists
Caller can arrive as any user
hops.why_cut: One wildcarded S_RFCACL grant is what lets the inbound call choose its identity. Remove it and every trust route into this system dies at once, however many destinations exist.

hops.name: Arrival identity is privileged
Transport is unauthenticated or unencrypted

paths.name: RFC callback inversion
paths.summary: Production's own outbound RFC call becomes the inbound route: the callee calls back on destination BACK, in the context of the production user who made the call.
paths.narrative: Directionality is a real property, not decoration. An OUTBOUND destination from production to a weaker system is an INBOUND risk, and neither row is alarming alone — which is exactly the class of risk a flat finding list structurally cannot show.

hops.name: Outbound route to a less-protected system
Callback protection not enforced
hops.why_cut: rfc/callback_security_method = 3 plus a per-destination allowlist rejects the callback outright. Until this check existed the path's only cut was unasserted — the graph could show the path but never show it closed.

hops.name: Remote callable surface is unrestricted
hops.why_cut: Activating UCON constrains which function modules are remotely callable at all, which severs the path higher up and more broadly than the callback allowlist.

hops.name: Caller's S_RFC is broad
RFC authorization check weakened

paths.name: Transport-borne code into production
paths.summary: Developer privilege in a lower system becomes arbitrary ABAP running in production, carried by the change process itself.
paths.narrative: Every hop is also a change-management control failure, so one path object serves the security buyer and the audit buyer at once. Note that a four-eyes violation is a GOVERNANCE rule, not a technical vulnerability, and it is still a genuine cut — a path model that cannot express process controls as edges would miss it.

hops.name: Route delivers straight to production
hops.why_cut: Removing the direct delivery route forces every change through the intermediate system, which is the cheapest and most auditable single change available.

hops.name: Release and import are not segregated
hops.why_cut: Four-eyes separation on release and import severs the path even where the route remains — a process control acting as a cut edge.

hops.name: Production accepts changes
Runtime authorization can be bypassed
Change is not attributable

paths.name: Exposed surface to OS command execution
paths.summary: An unauthenticated gateway, router, message server or ICF service reaches OS-level command execution, and from there the database.
paths.narrative: The closest analogue to the cloud archetype — internet, workload, privilege, data — and therefore the one to lead with for a CISO who already thinks in those terms. The entry conditions are CISA-cited rather than asserted.

hops.name: Unauthenticated entry point exposed
hops.why_cut: A deny-all default in reginfo/secinfo severs the entire gateway branch in one change; deactivating one ICF node severs the web branch. The permit-all and unrestricted-registration checks are cited here too: they name the condition this hop models, and citing only the missing-deny-all checks understated the hop's evidence and kept its CRITICAL findings out of choke-point ranking entirely.

hops.name: OS command execution reachable
hops.why_cut: Withdrawing S_LOG_COM / the external command definition removes the bridge from the application layer to the operating system.
hops.note: Custom ABAP that builds an OS command from external input is a way this hop becomes reachable without any gateway or job misconfiguration — the code IS the mechanism. ABAP-CMDI-* comes from our own scanner, ATC-CMDI from SAP's.

hops.name: Database is reachable and privileged
Activity would not be recorded

paths.name: Cloud identity into the on-premise backend
paths.summary: A weak BTP identity control reaches an ABAP backend through the Cloud Connector.
paths.narrative: The RISE-specific path, and the one where the incumbent framing of SAP security as ABAP-only is weakest. Modelled as a path, 'no MFA in IAS' stops being a medium-severity checkbox and becomes the first hop of a chain that ends in an on-premise user context.

hops.name: Cloud identity is weakly controlled
Credential or binding is exposed
Cloud Connector reaches the backend broadly
hops.why_cut: Narrowing one wildcard resource mapping cuts every path through that backend at once, whatever else is misconfigured upstream.

hops.name: Connector itself is vulnerable

paths.name: Business-impact path — no exploit required
paths.summary: One person can both create a vendor and pay one. No vulnerability is involved at any step.
paths.narrative: The path a cloud CNAPP cannot express at all, because in SAP the crown jewel is not a bucket of PII — it is a business transaction. This is computed at permission level, matching authorization object, field and activity rather than transaction code alone, which is what suppresses the display-only false positives.

hops.name: A user holds conflicting duties
hops.why_cut: Withdrawing one side of the conflict from one role removes the combination. The conflict IS the path.

hops.name: No compensating control is in force
hops.why_cut: A valid, unexpired mitigating control severs the business path without changing a single authorization.

hops.name: Financial controls are permissive
hops.note: FIN-SF-001 and FIN-DOC-001 replace FIN-DUAL-001 and FIN-CHG-001, which this hop cited for the life of the template and which no module has ever emitted. The names line up with what the phantoms were reaching for — dual control on payment-relevant master-data fields, and whether payment-relevant document fields stay editable after posting — so the hop is evidenced now rather than quietly short of two of its five checks. It stays a NON-cut: dual control on a bank field does not sever a path whose mechanism is one person holding conflicting duties. It makes the conflict harder to exploit, which is exactly what a non-cut hop is for.

hops.name: Activity would not be reviewed

paths.name: ABAP to operating system bridge
paths.summary: An external OS command definition plus a job that invokes it, in a system where the customer contractually has no OS access.
paths.narrative: RISE-specific and underrated. SAP's contract states plainly that customers never get OS access to managed servers — yet a customer-visible ABAP object that executes operating-system commands crosses exactly that boundary. The command and the job are modelled as separate objects so the edge between them is derivable.

hops.name: An external OS command is defined
hops.why_cut: Removing or parameter-locking the command definition closes the bridge regardless of who could have invoked it.

hops.name: Something can invoke it
It runs as a privileged identity

paths.name: Database-layer read beneath the ABAP authorization model
paths.summary: A principal holding privileges in the HANA database reads business data directly, below the layer where every S/4HANA access control is enforced.
paths.narrative: S/4HANA's authorization model lives in the ABAP layer. A database principal is not subject to it: no S_TABU_DIS check applies, no analytic privilege narrows the rows, and no Read Access Log records the read. The estate can be flawless at the application layer and this path still holds. It is also the route to the one loss scenario the model prices and the graph previously never reached — a path list that ends only in privilege and fraud implies data exfiltration is not modelled, which is the wrong thing for a report to imply.

hops.name: A database principal exists outside the ABAP layer
hops.note: Not a cut. Deactivating SYSTEM and DBADMIN is worth doing and does not disconnect anything: the path needs SOME database principal, and an estate always has several.

hops.name: Its privileges reach business data directly
hops.why_cut: Revoking the data-reaching grants leaves the principal without a route to the rows. _SYS_BI_CP_ALL is the one to revoke first and the reason this hop is a cut at all: it defeats analytic privileges outright, so a user restricted to one company code in every calculation view reads all of them. DEBUG / ATTACH DEBUGGER belongs here for the same reason — attaching to a session reads the data that session holds, whatever the grants say.

hops.name: A second, unmasked copy of the same data exists
hops.why_cut: Masking the non-production copy removes the data from that system, severing the branch that reaches production content through a system with non-production controls — without touching production. DPP-MASK-002 is the sharper of the two: it names systems identified as production COPIES, where the data is not merely similar but the same.

hops.name: The data is readable where it rests
hops.note: Backup encryption is the one that most often decides the loss magnitude rather than the likelihood: a backup is the copy that leaves the estate by design, on media the SAP controls do not follow. These checks name no object because they are properties of the system, so this hop contributes no nodes to the graph.

hops.name: The channel to the database is unprotected
hops.note: Cross-database (MDC) access matters here specifically: it turns a tenant boundary into a reachable one, so a principal in a non-production tenant is adjacent to the production tenant's data.

hops.name: The read would not be recorded
hops.note: A read leaves no trace by default. Table change logging records writes, not reads, which is why Read Access Logging is named separately — for exfiltration it is the only control on this list that would have produced evidence.

paths.name: Emergency access without accountability
paths.summary: A firefighter ID grants unrestricted privilege on demand, and the review that makes that acceptable is performed by nobody, or by the person who used it.
paths.narrative: Emergency access is not a misconfiguration — it is a designed control, and the privilege is meant to be available. It stays a control only while an independent controller reviews what was done with it. Where the reviewer is the user, the design has inverted: the account with the highest privilege in the estate carries the least oversight, and it does so with an approved process wrapped around it. This is the path an auditor recognises fastest, because every finding on it is a control failure rather than a vulnerability, and it is the reason a path model cannot be built out of CVEs.

hops.name: Emergency access is granted and used
hops.note: Deliberately not a cut. Withdrawing emergency access is not a remediation anyone will accept, and proposing it is how a report loses the reader.

hops.name: Nobody independent reviews what it did
hops.why_cut: Restoring an independent controller and an enforced log review returns emergency access to being a control, which severs the path without withdrawing anyone's access or changing a single authorization. This is the cheapest cut in the whole path list and the one most likely to be actioned.

hops.name: The grant itself bypassed approval
hops.why_cut: Requiring an approver other than the requester stops the assignment being made at all, which is higher up the path than reviewing it afterwards. Self-approval is the specific case: the workflow ran, and it ran with one person in every role.

hops.name: The risk it carries was never computed
hops.note: A disabled critical risk in the rule set is the quiet one: the analysis runs, reports clean, and the conflict it was built to catch was switched off upstream. An empty result and a suppressed result read identically in every report that does not check for this.

hops.name: The activity would not appear in the audit log
hops.note: rsau/enable off, or enabled with no active filter, are different failures with the same effect. Integrity protection matters more here than elsewhere: the privilege on this path is sufficient to edit the log it would appear in.

paths.name: Integration edge to backend function
paths.summary: An endpoint that authenticates nobody reaches an RFC-enabled function in the backend, over a destination that authenticates as a stored technical user.
paths.narrative: The integration layer is where the authorization model is most often traded for throughput. A proxy in pass-through mode applies no policy by definition, and the destination behind it logs on as a technical account, so an anonymous request arrives in the backend already privileged. Neither end is misconfigured on its own terms — the proxy is doing what a proxy does and the destination is doing what a destination does — which is why this is invisible to any review that looks at one system at a time.

hops.name: An endpoint accepts requests without authenticating them
hops.why_cut: Attaching an authentication policy at the proxy, or an auth handler to the service binding, ends the anonymous branch outright. It is a change on the edge and needs no backend change, which is what makes it the cut rather than the authorization work behind it.

hops.name: It reaches a callable backend function
hops.note: A wildcard OAuth scope and a deprecated grant type belong on the same hop for different reasons: the first decides how much the token is worth, the second how easily one is obtained. The resource-owner-password grant in particular turns any harvested user credential into an API token.

hops.name: The call carries a stored, shared credential
hops.why_cut: Principal propagation makes the backend see the real caller, so an anonymous request at the edge no longer arrives as a privileged technical user. It severs the path at the point where the caller's identity is currently discarded — which is also the point that makes the activity attributable afterwards.

hops.name: Events fan out beyond the intended consumer
hops.note: A wildcard topic subscription and a wildcard IDOC message type are the same defect in two technologies twenty years apart: the consumer decides what it receives, rather than the producer deciding what it releases. Unsigned webhooks add the inbound direction — without HMAC verification the endpoint cannot tell our own event from anyone else's.

hops.name: The traffic is not monitored
hops.note: These checks name no object — they are properties of the monitoring configuration, not of an integration — so this hop adds no nodes.

paths.name: Stored credential over an unprotected channel
paths.summary: A technical user's credential is stored for a destination that offers no transport protection, between two systems whose trust relationship is exactly what the credential unlocks.
paths.narrative: This path states a precondition the others do not, and states it rather than assuming it: an adversary must already hold a position on the network between the two systems. No configuration export can show that, and we do not claim it — what the export shows is the cryptographic condition and the trust the credential would yield, and the exposure zone recorded against each system is what tells a reader whether the precondition is plausible in their estate. It is modelled at all because SAP's own Secure Operations Map treats transport protection as a control in its own right rather than as defence in depth, and because the credential on this path is typically a technical user with wide authorization and no interactive logon to notice.

hops.name: A credential is stored for an unprotected channel
hops.why_cut: SNC on the RFC destination, or TLS verification on the BTP destination, protects the credential in flight. The credential can stay exactly where it is, which is what makes this actionable in a landscape where removing stored logons breaks interfaces nobody owns any more.

hops.name: Transport protection is weak where it is enabled
hops.note: Deliberately excludes CRYPTO-SNCECS-000. That finding says the SNC posture COULD NOT BE ASSESSED from the export supplied, and a hop that holds because we cannot see would let a path instantiate on our own blind spot. Missing evidence is reported as coverage, never as evidence.

hops.name: The trust anchors cannot be relied on
hops.note: An expired certificate usually presents as an outage rather than a breach — its risk here is the workaround it provokes, because verification switched off to restore an interface is rarely switched back on.

hops.name: The credential unlocks a trust relationship
hops.why_cut: Migrating the trust relationship to the current security method, and removing the fixed logon user from the trusted destination, means a captured credential no longer yields a logon in the target. Self-trust is the case worth naming: a system that trusts itself turns any callback into an authenticated session.

paths.name: Payee bank redirection
paths.summary: A payee's bank account is changed, the field that decides where money goes is not under dual control, and the change leaves little trail.
paths.narrative: The oldest SAP fraud there is. It needs no vulnerability, no privilege escalation and no code, and every step is a legitimate business transaction performed by an account entitled to perform it — which is why it is invisible to any tool reasoning about CVEs and roles alone. It is deliberately distinct from the segregation-of-duties path: that one asks whether one person holds conflicting duties, this one asks whether the specific field that decides the destination of a payment is protected, and those fail independently. An estate can pass SoD analysis and still hold this path.

hops.name: Payee bank details are being changed
hops.note: Not a cut, and not by itself a finding of fraud. Bank details change for ordinary reasons; the path is what surrounds the change, not the change.

hops.name: The field is not under dual control
hops.why_cut: Sensitive-field control (T055F) requires a second person to confirm a bank-detail change before it is effective for payment. It severs the path precisely at the step that decides where the money goes, and it does so without changing anyone's roles — which is why it succeeds where the SoD remediation on SAPPATH-06 stalls.

hops.name: The change bypassed the application layer
hops.why_cut: Withdrawing direct table maintenance on the bank-detail tables forces every change through the transaction that enforces dual control. A control in the application layer is not a control if the table underneath it can be edited directly, so this cut is what makes the dual-control cut above hold.

hops.name: One account is shared by several payees
hops.note: Legitimate for a factoring arrangement or a shared service centre, and a classic redirection signature otherwise. It is on the path as corroboration, never as the finding on its own.

hops.name: The trail is thin
hops.note: rec/client unset is the master switch: with it off, table change logging is inactive regardless of what each table's own setting says, so a table that looks logged is not.

paths.name: Gateway ACL to program execution on the host
paths.summary: An unauthenticated gateway accepts a rogue RFC server registration, or starts an external program, and the program runs on the application-server host.
paths.narrative: This is the condition CISA AA19-122A describes as 10KBLAZE, and it is the one path in this list that never touches the ABAP authorization model — the gateway is a network service, and a program it starts or accepts a registration from runs with the rights of the SAP system user on the host. That is what makes it distinct from the exposed-surface path rather than a variant of it: that path reaches the operating system through an ABAP bridge and can be cut by withdrawing S_LOG_COM, and this one cannot, because no ABAP authority is checked at any step. The two share a fix at the gateway and share nothing else.

hops.name: The gateway accepts what it should refuse
hops.why_cut: reginfo and secinfo with a deny-all default and specific permits are the whole control. It is a file change on the gateway host, needs no ABAP transport and no downtime beyond a gateway restart, which makes it the cheapest cut on any CRITICAL path here. A permit-all rule (P TP=* HOST=* USER=*) is the exact 10KBLAZE condition rather than an approximation of it.

hops.name: The ACL is not enforced at all
hops.why_cut: gw/acl_mode makes the gateway apply reginfo and secinfo even when a rule file is absent. Without it a correct ACL is only as durable as the file, and the failure mode is silent: remove the file and the control is gone with no error anywhere.

hops.name: A rogue application server can join the instance
hops.why_cut: ms/acl_info restricting registration to known hosts stops a rogue application server joining, which is the variant of this path that survives a correct gateway ACL — a server inside the instance is past the gateway rather than in front of it.

hops.name: The host reaches the database
hops.note: Where this path meets SAPPATH-08: execution on the host is adjacent to the database, and what it yields there is decided by the grants on that path rather than by anything on this one.

hops.name: Nothing would record it
hops.note: The Security Audit Log records ABAP events. A registered program that never logs on to ABAP produces none, which is why gateway logging (gw/logging) is the control that would actually have seen this — and no export we read today carries it.

paths.name: Unpatched, actively exploited, and reachable without credentials
paths.summary: A note SAP has published, for a vulnerability someone is already exploiting, on a surface that asks for no logon.
paths.narrative: The library had thirteen paths and none of them was the ordinary one. Every other path here is a configuration argument — conditions that co-exist and together permit something. This one is a missing patch, which is the plainest statement a security product can make and the one an executive already understands. It is also the only path whose cut SAP has already written: the note exists, it is published, and applying it removes the vulnerability rather than compensating for it. CVE-2025-31324 is cited in this file's own sources and no template used it.

hops.name: A published fix is missing
hops.why_cut: Applying the note removes the vulnerability rather than making it harder to reach, which no other cut in this library does — the rest reduce exposure to a defect that remains. HOTNEWS-003 is the one to apply first: it names notes for vulnerabilities that are being exploited now, not ones that might be.

hops.name: It needs no credentials
hops.note: This is what separates this path from a patch backlog. An unpatched note requiring a privileged logon is a queue item; one exploitable by anybody who can reach the port is an open door, and the two should not be read at the same urgency. Not a cut, because the vulnerability's own precondition is not something a customer can change — only the note or the exposure can move.

hops.name: The vulnerable surface is exposed
hops.why_cut: Deactivating the ICF node, or putting an authentication policy on the endpoint, removes the route to the vulnerable code while the note is still outstanding. That matters operationally: applying a note needs a maintenance window and a regression test, and closing a service does not. It is the cut a customer can take this afternoon.

hops.name: Reaching it yields privileged execution
hops.note: What the vulnerability is worth once used. A remote-code defect on a host that also holds an OS-command bridge and an active database superuser is a different loss from the same defect on a hardened one.

hops.name: The attempt would not be seen
hops.note: Actively-exploited means attempts are being made against estates like this one. Whether yours would produce a record is therefore a live question rather than a hypothetical.

paths.name: Custom code is the vulnerability
paths.summary: A Z-program with an injectable defect, callable from outside, with no authority check in front of it.
paths.narrative: This product ships a custom-code scanner — 133 rules, a statement lexer and taint analysis — and until now no path used a single one of its findings. That is a strange omission for an estate where the code is written by the customer: SAP's own defects arrive with a note and a fix, and these do not. The cut here is a code change rather than a configuration change, which makes it the slowest to close in the library and the only one no parameter can compensate for.

hops.name: Custom code carries an injectable defect
hops.why_cut: Fixing the statement removes the defect, and nothing else does. A parameter can narrow who reaches a program; none can make a concatenated SQL string safe. Note that both this scanner's findings and SAP's own ATC results appear here — where the customer already licenses ATC, its verdict is authoritative and duplicating it would only disagree with SAP about SAP's own tool.

hops.name: Nothing checks the caller's authority
hops.why_cut: An AUTHORITY-CHECK in the program means the caller must hold the object before the defect is reachable at all. It severs the path without fixing the defect, which is what makes it worth having: it is a change a Basis team can transport in days, where the code fix waits on the team that owns the program.

hops.name: The program is reachable from outside
hops.note: Custom code with no external caller is still a defect and is not this path. The scanner reports it either way; the path exists to say which ones have a route to them.

hops.name: The customer's own tooling already said so
hops.note: An unresolved ATC finding is a different argument from one this scanner discovered: SAP's tool raised it, somebody saw it, and it is still open. That is a governance fact rather than a technical one, and it is usually the more persuasive half.

hops.name: The transport route carries it to production
hops.note: How the defect arrives, rather than what it does. Present here because a code path that reaches production through an open change option is one nobody had to approve.

paths.name: A business role opens the data underneath it
paths.summary: An S/4HANA business role assigned in production, over a CDS view or an OData service that does not check authorization at all.
paths.narrative: The S/4HANA authorization model is business roles over business catalogs over CDS views, and a restriction at the top means nothing if the view underneath it was built with authorization checking switched off. This is the one path in the library that is specific to S/4HANA rather than to SAP generally — classic ABAP authorization objects do not have this shape, and an estate migrated from ECC inherits the roles without inheriting this exposure.

hops.name: A super-admin business role is live in production
hops.why_cut: SAP ships the SAP_BR_ADMINISTRATOR templates for configuration, not for production use, and says so. Withdrawing the template — or narrowing a restriction field left at 'Unrestricted' — is a role change rather than a code or platform change, and it is the step this path cannot survive.

hops.name: Authorization is switched off below the role
hops.why_cut: A CDS view annotated to skip authorization, or an OData V4 service group published without any, defeats whatever the role above it restricts — the check that would have narrowed the rows simply does not run. Re-enabling it restores every restriction already defined, which is why this is the cheaper of the two cuts even though it is the deeper one.

hops.name: Platform roles are over-assigned too
hops.note: The same failure a layer out: a Cloud Connector mapping without principal propagation, or a Cloud Foundry platform role handed to more people than administer the platform. Neither is required for this path and both widen who can walk it.

hops.name: The read would leave no trace
hops.note: Shares its ending with the database-layer path: a read is not a change, so table change logging never sees it, and Read Access Logging is the only control on this list that would have produced evidence.

paths.name: A RISE communication arrangement as the front door
paths.summary: A communication arrangement with weak or absent authentication, carrying more scope than it needs, in front of published services.
paths.narrative: Communication arrangements are how a RISE tenant is integrated, and they are configured by the customer rather than by SAP — which puts them squarely on the customer's side of the shared-responsibility line and makes them the most RISE-specific exposure in this product. An arrangement is a named user, a scope and an endpoint in one object, so a weak one is simultaneously a credential problem, an authorization problem and an exposure problem, and reading it as any one of those understates it.

hops.name: An arrangement authenticates weakly or not at all
hops.why_cut: Certificate-based authentication on the arrangement ends the anonymous and shared-secret routes in one change, and it is a change the customer can make: the arrangement is theirs to configure under RISE, unlike the parameters SAP holds.

hops.name: It carries more scope than it needs
hops.why_cut: Narrowing the scenario list, or giving each arrangement its own communication user rather than sharing one across many, means a compromised arrangement reaches only what it was built for. It severs the path from the arrangement to everything else the shared user could do.

hops.name: Sensitive services are published behind it
hops.note: What the arrangement reaches. Published OData and SOAP surfaces are the point of an arrangement, so this hop is never a cut — removing it removes the integration, which is not remediation.

hops.name: Identity trust is loose around it
hops.note: SAP's default IDP trust left active, or automatic shadow-user creation, means an identity from outside the corporate directory can become a user here. It widens who reaches the arrangement rather than what the arrangement reaches.
